title: Profit and Loss
subtitle: Quantitative Aptitude – Placement Preparation
description: Learn cost price, selling price, profit, loss, marked price, discount, successive changes, false weights and placement shortcuts through formulas and solved examples.
learningObjectives: Understand cost price, selling price, marked price, profit and loss.
Calculate profit percentage and loss percentage.
Find cost price or selling price when percentage gain or loss is given.
Handle successive discounts and successive profit or loss.
Differentiate percentages calculated on cost price and selling price.
Apply placement shortcuts accurately and quickly.

sections.heading: 1. Basic Terms
content: Cost Price (CP) is the price at which an article is purchased.
Selling Price (SP) is the price at which an article is sold.
Marked Price (MP) is the price printed or displayed before discount.
Profit occurs when SP is greater than CP.
Loss occurs when SP is less than CP.

examples.question: An article is bought for ₹800 and sold for ₹950. Find the profit.
An article is bought for ₹1,200 and sold for ₹1,050. Find the loss.

sections.heading: 2. Profit Percentage and Loss Percentage
content: Profit percentage and loss percentage are normally calculated on cost price unless stated otherwise.
Always identify the correct base before applying a percentage.

examples.question: An article is bought for ₹500 and sold for ₹600. Find the profit percentage.
An article is bought for ₹800 and sold for ₹680. Find the loss percentage.

sections.heading: 3. Finding Selling Price
content: When cost price and profit or loss percentage are known, selling price can be found directly.
A profit increases cost price, while a loss decreases it.
formulas: SP at x% profit = CP × (100 + x) / 100
SP at x% loss = CP × (100 − x) / 100

examples.question: Find the selling price of an article costing ₹1,500 at a profit of 20%.
Find the selling price of an article costing ₹2,400 at a loss of 15%.

sections.heading: 4. Finding Cost Price
content: When selling price and profit or loss percentage are known, reverse the multiplier to find cost price.
formulas: CP when sold at x% profit = SP × 100 / (100 + x)
CP when sold at x% loss = SP × 100 / (100 − x)

examples.question: An article is sold for ₹1,440 at a profit of 20%. Find the cost price.
An article is sold for ₹1,700 at a loss of 15%. Find the cost price.

sections.heading: 5. Marked Price and Discount
content: Discount is the reduction offered on marked price.
The customer pays the selling price after discount.
Discount percentage is calculated on marked price.
formulas: SP after x% discount = MP × (100 − x) / 100

examples.question: An article marked at ₹2,000 is sold at a discount of 15%. Find the selling price.
An article is sold for ₹1,800 after a 10% discount. Find the marked price.

sections.heading: 6. Discount and Profit Together
content: In many placement questions, an article is marked above cost price and then sold at a discount.
Apply markup first to get marked price, then apply discount to get selling price.

examples.question: A shopkeeper marks an article 25% above cost price and gives a 10% discount. Find the profit percentage.
An article costing ₹800 is marked 40% above cost and sold at a discount of 20%. Find the selling price and profit percentage.

sections.heading: 7. Successive Discounts
content: Successive discounts are applied one after another, not added directly.
The second discount is calculated on the reduced price after the first discount.
formulas: Equivalent discount for a% and b% = a + b − ab/100

examples.question: Find the single equivalent discount of 20% followed by 10%.
An article marked at ₹5,000 gets successive discounts of 20% and 10%. Find the final selling price.

sections.heading: 8. Successive Profit and Loss
content: When multiple percentage changes occur, multiply their factors.
Do not simply add profit and loss percentages.
A gain of x% followed by a loss of x% always results in a net loss.
formulas: Net percentage change for a% and b% = a + b + ab/100, using negative signs for losses
Equal gain and loss of x% gives net loss = x²/100%

examples.question: A price increases by 20% and then decreases by 10%. Find the net percentage change.
An article is sold at 20% profit and later the price is reduced by 20%. Find the net result relative to cost price.

sections.heading: 9. Profit Based on Selling Price
content: Sometimes profit is stated as a percentage of selling price instead of cost price.
Read the wording carefully because the base changes.
formulas: If profit is x% of SP, then CP = SP × (100 − x)/100
If profit is x% of SP, profit % on CP = x/(100 − x) × 100

examples.question: Profit is 20% of selling price. Find the profit percentage on cost price.
examples.solution: Assume SP = ₹100. Profit = ₹20, so CP = ₹80. Profit % on CP = 20/80 × 100 = 25%.

examples.question: A trader sells an article for ₹1,000 and profit is 15% of SP. Find CP.

sections.heading: 10. Loss Based on Selling Price
content: If loss is expressed as a percentage of selling price, convert it carefully to a percentage of cost price.
formulas: If loss is x% of SP, then CP = SP × (100 + x)/100

examples.question: Loss is 20% of selling price. Find the loss percentage on cost price.
examples.solution: Assume SP = ₹100. Loss = ₹20, so CP = ₹120. Loss % on CP = 20/120 × 100 = 16⅔%.

sections.heading: 11. Selling Two Articles at Same Selling Price
content: If two articles are sold at the same selling price, one at x% gain and the other at x% loss, there is always an overall loss.
This shortcut applies only when both selling prices are equal and the gain and loss percentages are equal.

examples.question: Two articles are sold for ₹1,200 each. One is sold at 20% profit and the other at 20% loss. Find the overall loss percentage.

sections.heading: 12. Selling Two Articles at Same Cost Price
content: If two articles have the same cost price, one sold at x% gain and the other at x% loss, the gains and losses cancel.
The overall result is neither profit nor loss.

examples.question: Two articles cost ₹1,000 each. One is sold at 15% profit and the other at 15% loss. Find the overall result.
examples.solution: Profit on first = ₹150. Loss on second = ₹150. Net result = no profit and no loss.

sections.heading: 13. Required Selling Price for a Desired Profit
content: Sometimes an article is sold at a loss and the question asks how much more it should be sold for to earn a profit.
First find cost price, then calculate the desired selling price.

examples.question: An article is sold for ₹960 at a loss of 20%. At what price should it be sold to gain 25%?

sections.heading: 14. Change in Selling Price and Change in Profit
content: For a fixed cost price, any increase in selling price directly increases profit by the same amount.
Any decrease in selling price directly reduces profit or increases loss by the same amount.

examples.question: A trader earns ₹240 profit by selling an article for ₹1,440. What would the profit be if it were sold for ₹1,560?

sections.heading: 15. False Weight and Dishonest Dealer
content: A dishonest dealer may charge for a full kilogram but give less than one kilogram.
Even when goods are sold at cost price, the shortage in weight creates a profit.
Use actual quantity given as the effective cost base.
formulas: Profit % when x grams are given instead of 1000 grams at cost price = [(1000 − x) / x] × 100
If a dealer uses a weight that is x% less, profit % = x/(100 − x) × 100

examples.question: A dealer gives 900 grams instead of 1 kilogram and charges the cost price of 1 kilogram. Find the profit percentage.
examples.solution: Assume CP of 1 kg = ₹100. CP of 900 g = ₹90, but SP = ₹100. Profit = ₹10. Profit % = 10/90 × 100 = 11⅑%.

examples.question: A dealer uses an 800-gram weight for 1 kilogram and sells at cost price. Find the profit percentage.

sections.heading: 16. False Weight with Markup or Discount
content: When false weight is combined with markup or discount, calculate the effective selling price and the actual cost of quantity delivered.

examples.question: A dealer marks goods 20% above cost, gives a 10% discount and uses a 900-gram weight for 1 kilogram. Find the profit percentage.
examples.solution: Assume CP of 1 kg = ₹100. Marked price = ₹120. After 10% discount, SP charged = ₹108. Actual CP of 900 g = ₹90. Profit = ₹18. Profit % = 18/90 × 100 = 20%.

sections.heading: 17. Break-Even Discount
content: The break-even discount is the maximum discount that can be offered without profit or loss when an article is marked above cost price.
formulas: If markup is x%, break-even discount % = x/(100 + x) × 100

examples.question: An article is marked 25% above cost price. What maximum discount can be given without loss?

sections.heading: 18. Ratio Method
content: The ratio method is often faster than using full formulas.
At x% profit, CP:SP = 100:(100 + x).
At x% loss, CP:SP = 100:(100 − x).

examples.question: An article is sold at 25% profit. If SP is ₹1,500, find CP using ratio.

quickShortcuts.title: Profit and loss base
quickShortcuts.note: Unless stated otherwise, profit percentage and loss percentage are calculated on cost price.

quickShortcuts.title: Profit multiplier
quickShortcuts.note: At x% profit, multiply CP by (100 + x)/100.

quickShortcuts.title: Loss multiplier
quickShortcuts.note: At x% loss, multiply CP by (100 − x)/100.

quickShortcuts.title: Successive discounts
quickShortcuts.note: Equivalent discount of a% and b% is a + b − ab/100.

quickShortcuts.title: Equal gain and loss
quickShortcuts.note: An x% gain followed by an x% loss gives x²/100% loss.

quickShortcuts.title: Same selling price shortcut
quickShortcuts.note: If two articles are sold at the same SP, one at x% gain and the other at x% loss, overall loss is x²/100%.

quickShortcuts.title: Marked price route
quickShortcuts.note: Calculate MP from CP first, then apply discount to get SP.

quickShortcuts.title: False weight
quickShortcuts.note: When x grams are given instead of 1000 grams, profit % is (1000 − x)/x × 100.

quickShortcuts.title: Break-even discount
quickShortcuts.note: For x% markup, maximum no-loss discount is x/(100 + x) × 100.

quickShortcuts.title: Ratio method
quickShortcuts.note: At x% profit use CP:SP = 100:(100+x); at x% loss use 100:(100−x).

commonMistakes: Calculating profit percentage on selling price instead of cost price.
Calculating discount percentage on cost price instead of marked price.
Assuming equal profit and loss percentages cancel in all cases.
Using the same-selling-price shortcut when selling prices are not equal.
Ignoring the actual reduced quantity in false-weight questions.
Applying discount before calculating marked price when the markup is given on cost price.
Confusing profit amount with profit percentage.
Using 100 − x in the denominator for profit instead of loss.
Forgetting that a percentage change must be applied to the current value at each stage.
